rv.q: Shuffling into view in a heavy overcoat and hat, with pin-striped brown suit beneath, wielding a walking cane and old-world, European-accented courtesy, Suchet’s grizzled Jewish eccentric is a witty and wise veteran of multiple transactions and survivor of many traumas. He’s been married three – or is it four?
This revival – a transfer from the Theatre Royal Bath – suggests it’s a genuinely good play, albeit not as good as Miller’s better-known output.

David Suchet’s peerless performance, flavoured with a masterful spiel that puts his character squarely (and knowingly) in the traditions of Jewish comedy, has such bravado insouciance that everything else somehow falls before it.
What's more The Price 's cry from the heart about a world where money rules and distorts all meaning feels more relevant now than ever.
The whole cast makes Miller's vision utterly compelling: the costs of belief in the American Dream have rarely been so acutely presented.
Unfortunately, however, this incredible set design is underserved by the direction and acting.

cn.t: Miller's rarity gets a powerful revival led by David Suchet's brilliant, comedic turn, though the play itself divides critics on its enduring appeal.
